stem: A 16-year-old seeks testing and treatment for a suspected sexually transmitted infection and asks whether parental consent is required. Which response is most accurate?

options.A: Federal law requires parental consent for all STI testing and treatment of minors, so care cannot begin until a parent authorizes it.
options.B: All 50 states and the District of Columbia allow minors to consent for their own STI services; confidentiality, notification, and some age- or service-specific provisions still vary, so current jurisdiction law and policy must be applied.
options.C: Minors can consent to STI testing nationwide but never to treatment, so a parent must authorize medication in every jurisdiction.
options.D: Only emancipated minors may independently consent to STI services; non-emancipated adolescents always require a parent to be present.

rationale: CDC's current STI Treatment Guidelines state that all 50 states and the District of Columbia explicitly allow minors to consent for their own STI services and that no state requires parental consent for STI care. CDC also notes variation in age provisions for specified services and important confidentiality and parental-notification issues. B accurately combines the nationwide STI-consent principle with the need to apply current jurisdiction-specific details. A, C, and D impose universal restrictions that CDC says are incorrect.
educational_objective: Recognize minors' nationwide authority to consent for STI services while applying jurisdiction-specific confidentiality, notification, age, and service provisions at the point of care.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021 — Adolescents
source_version_date: 2021 guideline remains CDC's current STI Treatment Guidelines in 2026
source_locator: Adolescents — Legal Issues and Confidentiality; CDC STI Treatment Guidelines landing page identifying the 2021 guideline as current clinical guidance.
source_claim_supported: All 50 states and DC explicitly allow minors to consent for their own STI services; no state requires parental consent for STI care; age provisions for specified services and confidentiality/notification considerations vary.

source_original.stem: A 16-year-old seeks testing and treatment for a suspected sexually transmitted infection and asks whether parental consent is required. Which response is most accurate?

options.A: Federal law requires parental consent for all STI testing and treatment of minors, so care cannot begin until a parent authorizes it.
options.B: Minors can consent to STI services in every state and DC, but age, confidentiality, notification, and service-specific details can vary; apply current jurisdiction law and policy.
options.C: Minors can consent to STI testing nationwide but never to treatment, so a parent must authorize medication in every jurisdiction.
options.D: Only emancipated minors may independently consent to STI services; non-emancipated adolescents always require a parent to be present.

source_original.rationale: CDC states that every state and the District of Columbia explicitly allow minors to consent for their own STI services, while age provisions for some services and confidentiality or notification rules can vary. Therefore the nurse should recognize the general consent authority while applying current jurisdiction-specific law and policy and explaining confidentiality limits. The other options incorrectly impose universal parental-consent, testing-only, or emancipation requirements.
source_original.source_detail: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines — Adolescents, Legal Issues and Confidentiality: all 50 states and DC explicitly allow minors to consent for their own STI services; age provisions for some services and confidentiality/notification rules vary by jurisdiction. CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 remain the live CDC guideline in 2026; page and legal caveats rechecked 2026-08-15. Current state law/policy must be applied at the point of care. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: prioritization, continuity, confidentiality, quality/cost-effective care, legal/ethical rights and assignment/delegation activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained key and construct. Strengthened the exact CDC-supported nationwide statement by adding that no state requires parental consent for STI care in the rationale, while preserving jurisdiction-specific confidentiality/notification caveats and avoiding any claim of absolute confidentiality.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Minor consent and confidentiality for STI care
audit_findings.source_authority: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines plus current CDC adolescent-provider guidance.
audit_findings.currentness: CDC continues to identify the 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines as current in 2026.
audit_findings.claim_audit: Nationwide consent and no-parental-consent claim are direct CDC text; confidentiality is explicitly not portrayed as absolute.

distractor_audit.B: Matches CDC nationwide rule with jurisdiction caveats.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B is compatible with CDC's legal summary.
audit_findings.cueing: All choices address consent authority and no second answer is legally supportable under the cited CDC framework.
audit_findings.blueprint: Client rights/confidentiality/legal responsibilities under Management of Care.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked high-stakes legal wording and current CDC status; final item directs application of jurisdiction law rather than substituting CDC for legal advice.
